utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Ms. Chittenden, is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in the courtroom. Our first witness this morning is Witness 110, who will be known by the pseudonym of PW-043. He will be testifying with face and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please wait a moment -- no, please open the screens first. Good morning to you again, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now. Would you please read aloud the text on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please sit down. We have a problem. We didn't hear the English interpretation on channel 4. And not the B/C/S translation? No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We seem to have had a technical problem in the booth. Could the witness please repeat the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, because of technical problems please repeat the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now please sit down. I think you know the procedure in this Tribunal. There are still protective measures for you in place and your name will not be broadcast and your face and voice will not be seen and heard outside the courtroom. Ms. Chittenden has, I think, some questions for you. Please, Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: We met yesterday. My name is Caitlin Chittenden and I'll be asking you some questions today on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please could we have Exhibit P649 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see something coming up on the screen in front of you now. Please can you read it to yourself and confirm that that's your name written next to PW-043.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this into evidence as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall testifying in the case of Prosecutor versus Popovic et al. on 23 January 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Was your testimony at that time truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to listen to your Popovic testimony again before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, I had the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions again in court today, would you answer in the same way?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to offer the witness's testimony in Popovic into evidence. It is P647, which should be admitted under seal; and P648, the public version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received with the given numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would also like to offer into evidence the exhibits admitted in conjunction with this witness's testimony in the Popovic case. The first exhibit I would like to offer for admission is P650, under seal. This is the witness's statement to the OTP on 21 January 2007. This statement was admitted in Popovic as the underlying Rule 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should continue with the other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: The second exhibit I would like to offer is an intercept, it's P651. I would like to offer this into evidence as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. For the record, the third exhibit which was admitted via this witness's testimony in Popovic is an intercept at 1305 hours on 21 July 1995. This has already been admitted in this case through PW-032 as P269A. However, I would like to request that this be placed under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was that not received under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I don't believe it was, Your Honour. I would like to put this under seal, please, as well as P269C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was previously received under seal. I'm told that there's no need to do it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I would now like to read a short summary of the witness's testimony in Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, after I read out the summary, I'll have a few further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we may move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: As an intercept operator, the witness followed the established procedure at his unit for scanning, recording, and transcribing intercepts into notebooks. Normal practice was to work in two-hour shifts followed by a four-hour break, depending on how busy it was. The soldiers present were divided into two alternating groups, each of whom would be on duty for seven days and off duty for seven days. The witness remained in the ABiH until mid-October 1997. Your Honours, that concludes my summary. I now have a couple of questions I would like to put to the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to show you a booklet of two intercepts that we have compiled. For the record, these intercepts are Exhibit P651 and P269A.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please could I ask for the assistance of the Court Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, please could you take a moment to look through this booklet and let me know whether you recognise your handwriting on the two intercepts.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And can you check both of the intercepts for me behind tabs 1 and 2. It should just be the last page in the booklet there, if you turn to the very last page.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that is your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, were you the operator who recorded and transcribed these two intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I do not remember the conversations, but this is my handwriting so probably I was the operator.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Did you review these two intercepts before you testified in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I do not remember the first one and I did review the second one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a chance to look at this intercept booklet and these two intercepts yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I did review them yesterday, but I cannot seem to remember the first conversation. I do remember the second one if it's just what is on the last page here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you look at an original notebook yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: And did you see in that original notebook those conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I saw the original conversations. I remembered that I saw the second of these two, but I cannot seem to remember the first one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please could I ask for the assistance of the Court Usher. I will just pass you the original notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, please could you look at the bottom of the page on the right-hand side and let me know if that's your handwriting.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Now, in the booklet, the blue booklet, if you can turn to the intercept behind tab 1 and let me know if that's the same intercept as what's in the original notebook. So it's the intercept behind tab 1, not the one that you're looking at the moment in the book, but the first intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Please could I ask for the assistance of the Court Usher. Your Honours, if I just may turn to the page in the booklet for him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two are not the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Witness, just to be clear, I'd like you to look at that -- the first tab of the booklet, which is the intercept of 1242, P651; and the original notebook which you have in front of you, let me know if they're the same.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to have the original book -- notebook. The Chamber has seen it, the original, and could it be forwarded to Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic, please. Mr. Tolimir, yes, have a look. Do you have cross-examination for this witness? It's now your turn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May there be peace in this house for all those present and may God's will be done in these proceedings, and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish. I wish the witness a pleasant stay in The Hague. I will have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as you have a pseudonym, I will address you as "Mr. Witness." The Prosecutor read parts of your statement in open and closed sessions. I would just ask you this. In paragraph 5 in the first line --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please show the statement first, it's P560 [as interpreted], please, so that the witness can follow his own statement. Thank you. Thank you. We can see it now, we can see page 1 in the original language. Can we please move on to the second page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see paragraph 5. You stated that you came to the unit on the 30th of April, 1995, and that you were there until the 12th of February, 1996. My question is the following: Did you arrive to a place that was vacant or were you sent there because the manning levels were not adequate?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Can you please just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you arrive to the unit in April 1995 -- in 1994, to your unit, to a place that was vacated or because there was insufficient personnel of the adequate profile in your unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I came to the unit as a wounded soldier so I wouldn't go out to the front, and the unit was operative even before I got there. So it was not because of the manning levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 7, please have a look at it, you say in the first line that you were working two hours per shift and then would get four hours of rest. And that there would be two intercept operators in the room and that each of them had a set for himself, and that you worked on a device that scanned only one frequency. Did I quote properly what you said under item 7? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, you quoted what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is my question: Was the scope of your unit's work small and could you record, transcribe, process, and dispatch more than one, two, three, or four conversations during one two-hour shift? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: The scope of the work was not always the same. It could happen that there would be a number of conversations or for longer periods there would be nothing. We recorded the conversations and only then we would transcribe them as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How many conversations could you process during one two-hour shift in practice?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. It all depends on the length of a given conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 7 you say that the device only scanned one frequency. Can you tell us why and how this was possible and what were the technical characteristics of these devices? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I could not remember that now because I was not familiar with the devices before I got into my unit. I only knew about the devices what I learned from my predecessors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify for the record that what the statement in paragraph 7 actually says is: "I do not remember very well, but it seems to me that I was working on a device that scanned only one frequency." So that's not -- that's not quite the same as what was quoted on -- sorry, lines 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now really a quote, but what is the difference to the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: I apologise. The difference is in lines 10 and 11 the accused said the device only scanned one frequency, but the witness actually said he wasn't sure, but it seems that he was working on a device that scanned only one frequency. Just to be clear. I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, thanks also to Ms. Chittenden, she quoted your statement precisely now. So can you please now answer the question. Did the device that you worked with scan only one frequency? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I couldn't remember that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But when you wrote the statement - we see that it was recorded in 2007 - that was just what you said, that you do not precisely remember but that it scanned only one frequency. In the notes that you just had a chance to have a look at written in your handwriting, were all the conversations from one and the same frequency or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I did not review the entire notebook except for the conversations that have to do with this trial so that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It would be very important for us if you could remember why the device scanned only one frequency and whether all the other devices also scanned one frequency each? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I cannot remember about this device, but it was not the case that all devices were scanning only one frequency each.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could all the devices scan various frequencies within the radio network? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I know that some of them could, but I cannot remember about all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In any case, the one you worked with did scan frequencies, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that right now I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber when the device is not scanning a frequency, what do you do with it then? How do you choose a particular channel if it cannot scan the radio waves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I cannot remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That is sufficient. In paragraph 8, please have a look at it now. I will not quote it. I will just retell what it says there. In lines 4 and 5 you say that you remember that you only had one tape and that you would record new conversations over the ones that were already recorded once the tape was full. Is that correct or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us and answer my question by saying whether this one single tape satisfied the needs that you had? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: No, it did not meet our needs, but that was what we had and we had to work with it and do as much work as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same paragraph, in line 2, you say that your commander listened to all recorded conversations. Am I right, it's line 2: "The commander listened to all recorded conversations ..." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, but I really cannot remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me when did he listen to the recorded conversations, during your shift or after your shift ended? Do you remember how he used to do that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: When there was a conversation that we deemed to be interesting, then we would call him to check and establish whether it was transcribed in the same way as it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in the statement that he listened to all recorded conversations and not only when you called him. Is there now an inconsistency between what you're saying now and your statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Believe me, I cannot really remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember any situation in which the commander listened to a conversation you were recording and when did he do that, at the time of your shift or after your shift? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Well, I can, for example, remember that on one occasion I asked him to come and listen to a conversation because it was a fairly lengthy one and I was worried. I thought I might have missed something in the conversation, so I wanted him to listen to it to see that everything had been recorded correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time the commander would listen to recorded conversations, would you be able to use a band to -- a tape to record another conversation if there were participants in a conversation on a frequency that you were scanning?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Well, the tape I used, the device I used, couldn't be used to record another conversation while we were listening to a previous conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, I had to stop you again because you were overlapping and it's too fast for the interpreters. Now put the question to the witness that you wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear the interpretation of what you just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I asked you not to overlap, please, and wait until the answer is recorded. You were too fast. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I've received the interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the comment that the Presiding Judge has made. Please slow down a little, pause after my questions, and then we'll be able to proceed more efficiently. With regard to the information on participants, as you call them, did you record this information in log-books for each conversation? You mention this in item 9 if you can't remember this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I think that we noted down the details and that we had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: With regard to the notebook you had a look at, you mentioned what the Prosecution gave you, in that notebook is there the time of each conversation and the date of the conversation concerned? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: As far as I can see, given what I have before me, yes, that's noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you bring those notebooks with you from home or did you get them from the commander?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: We took the notebooks or we obtained the notebooks at work. We didn't carry them around.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they have any registration numbers? Were they assigned officially and so on and so forth? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the premises were there other users who performed the same sort of duties as your group? Were there other individuals who used these interception devices? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were they part of the structure of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or were they part of some other structure?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I wouldn't really know right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It's not that important. I'm asking you about that because you mentioned this sabotage group. You didn't mention any other users, and it would be natural for you to know if someone else is involved in interception -- well, it would be natural for you to communicate with them during a one-year period, but if you can't remember the details it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I'm not sure. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Usher will now return this notebook to you, the one that you used, as you said. You can have a look at it, and once you have done that please answer my following question -- or first, have a look at the notebook and then I will put my question to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. While you're having a look at it, have a look at the first page, the last page, the first few pages as well, and have a look at the conversations that you were involved in and have you noted the time and dates of those conversations? Can you see the dates and times of those conversations in the notebook? Thank you. Thank you. Please have a look at the conversations you are testifying about here. Are the dates and times noted by those conversations? Thank you. And does this correspond to the binder that you have next to you that was provided to you by the Usher?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: The time is there for all the conversations, but the dates were noted at the beginning of the day, not for each conversation. There were several conversations in the course of one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you all have such notebooks or similar notebooks -- or did you all have such notebooks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: We would obtain these notebooks at our work-place and we would hand the notebook to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was whether in your group that worked in the northern building or all those who intercepted conversations were people who used such notebooks, or were there other notebooks as well, or were there only those kinds of notebooks because the unit issued them?

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Initially you expressed doubts about the first conversation that you were presented. It was in the first binder in blue that the Usher gave you. Since you expressed such doubts -- well, did you have a look at that conversation yesterday when you were being proofed for your testimony? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: I saw this conversation, but in the list where the conversation was included there was something from another conversation. I didn't recognise it immediately. I thought that was part of the conversation that I had to deal with too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's a matter of confusion. There was a mistake. It's not a factual error.

utterances.speaker: PW-043
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for those answers. Thank you for appearing here. On behalf of my Defence I would like to thank you, and I wish you a nice stay here. I wish you a safe trip home.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I have now concluded my cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Ms. Chittenden, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHITTENDEN
utterances.text: No, I don't. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask the Court Usher to bring the notebook, the original notebook, again to the Bench. I would like to have a look at it again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, when you have a look at the notebook, bear in mind that it doesn't have a registration number and it's not even on the list which includes those registration numbers of other notebooks that were tendered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we all come to our findings at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have seen it and it should be returned to Ms. Chittenden. Thank you. Sir, this concludes your examination. The Chamber would like to thank you that you were able to come to The Hague again and to assist us. We -- you are now free to return to your normal activities and your place of residence, and again, thank you very much for your attendance. The next witness will be available as well? I think it is -- we have to arrange the system and the screen. Perhaps we should have a short break of ten minutes, and then we resume. The Court Usher will assist you after we have raised, and we will resume five minutes before 10.00. --- Break taken at 9.48 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, we have the witness we know already.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The gap-filler is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then he should brought in, please. I think the witness didn't expect ever to be called "gap-filler," but that happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please sit down. Good morning, Mr. Blaszczyk. I'm not sure if I -- if that is the right pronunciation. Welcome back again in this trial. May I remind you again that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your examination still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Tolimir, we are in the middle of the cross-examination. We started with that in April. Please examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to complete this testimony in accordance with God's will. Sir, quite some time has passed since we spoke to each other. We were speaking on the last occasion about the Drina Corps, about rotation, and I have a few questions that will take us to the heart of the matter that we were concerned with last time. First of all, let me ask you the following. When the collection of the Drina Corps arrived in the hands of the Prosecution, according to your statements and the documents that we have been provided with, documents that have been shown here by the Prosecution, well, the place of custody frequently changed. Did you investigate where the collection of the Drina Corps that you have testified about was taken to, which places it passed through? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since the Drina Corps collection arrived to The Hague, it was stored in evidence unit and was kept entire time over there. If anybody wanted to get particular document from the evidence unit, should fill out the form and sign this form and leave this form in evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That concerns its custody here, but my question was whether you launched a particular investigation into all the places to which the Drina Corps collection of documents was taken until it arrived in the hands of the Prosecution? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our investigation, the Drina Corps collection was first kept by VRS army, by the Drina Corps itself. It was collected -- documents from the Drina Corps collection were collected by Drina Corps in Vlasenica; and then transferred to Bijeljina, stayed in Bijeljina about one year. From Bijeljina again the entire collection was taken back to Sokolac. And then from Sokolac, on the order of Colonel Andric, was transferred to Mali Zvornik. And after that we got information that collection is in Gornji Milanovac, in Serbia. And then collection was handed over to the Joint Commission of RS MUP and RS MOD and taken to Banja Luka. For one day -- for few days were kept at the premises of RS MUP in Banja Luka, and on the 13th of December, 2004, was handed over to our field office, ICTY field office in Banja Luka. And of course then it was the process taking this collection through Zagreb to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how it was taken from Mali Zvornik to Milanovac? If you looked into the matter you could answer that question; if not, it doesn't matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our knowledge, the information we got from one of the witnesses, Nebojsa Vukicevic, when he came at one stage to Mali Zvornik to get more documents, the collection was not there. The collection -- according to information he got on the spot, the collection was taken away by member of the Army of Serbia and Montenegro. Whether it was taken directly to Gornji Milanovac or to other places, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you about that because the collection is not a small one, it can't be dealt with by just an individual, but that's not that important.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P134 on the screen now. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to come up on the screen I can say that we're waiting for photographs, photographs that have been shown to you already in the course of your testimony. Here they are. We can see that the documents are in bundles. They've been taken out of this box. Did each of the bundles have a binder which included a list of the relevant documents? Thank you. We can see some sort of a binder here that looks like a divider -- that looks like a log-book, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was whether each bundle of documents - and we can see the documents that have been taken out of the box - did each bundle contain a list of the documents or was there just one notebook where the list of documents -- a notebook such as the one we can see in the photograph, the notebook looks like a log-book. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seen this collection first time in Zagreb. It was few days after that the pictures were taken -- this picture was taken. And I don't remember on the -- on a list of the documents, you know, in particular binders. And as far as I know, looking at the collection later stage even, I didn't find any list. I didn't remember -- I don't remember any list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it common practice to keep the documents of an entire corps without having a list of the documents, and when you subsequently examined the collection did you come across a list of any kind, a list of any documents or at least a list for part of the documents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember from top of my head whether there is any list, but possible, possible there were few log-books where it -- where, for example, dispatches of telegram were recorded. Of course they are -- but from the top of my head I don't remember a list. And I didn't notice such lists in what is exactly in this collection entirely, so this collection, I didn't notice such list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether we can find a list of any part of the documents from the Drina Corps in the electronic system that we have? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe entire collection is accessible for the Defence also in the system, and including whatever is in -- also, if the analysis exist, the list are also accessible for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please answer my following question. Can this be a full and authentic collection if we don't have these lists of documents, and could you take documents from this collection before the collection arrived in the hands of the Prosecution? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand why this collection cannot be authenticated without a list. You know, the list doesn't say as anything about authentication about this collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Some of the documents were used, as has been said in the course of your testimony, in the Radislav Krstic case. The trial came to an end in 2001, in the -- the trial in the Krstic case. The appeals phase was completed in 2004. All of these documents were found when exactly? Could you please tell us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire collection was seized by the Joint Commission of RS MUP and RS MOD on the 9th of December, 2004, and it was handed over to ICTY in December 13, 2004, and came to The Hague, physically came to The Hague, it was beginning of January 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. So the appeals phase in the Krstic case was completed before this collection of documents was accessible to the Prosecution? Is that correct or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when appeal was completed for the Krstic case. Possible. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It's easy to check this in the Tribunal. Please have a look at that and tell me whether I'm correct when I say that the case was completed in 2004. I thought that you as an investigator looked into that too. I would like to ask you the following now. Last time a witness was here, a witness who saw this collection that you have called "Atlantida." He said that he never gave it that title. Can you tell us anything about this, the question -- the witness concerned is called Danko Gojkovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the answer of Danko Gojkovic, yes, confirming that during my interview with him also, that he didn't give this name of this binder, "Atlantida," to this part of the documents. And he never said -- and I think it's not -- Danko Gojkovic is not the man who created this binder. It could be done by another person. We have some guessing, of course, you know, who could create this binder, but the man who may create this binder refused to be interviewed by us. We tried to interview him, but he refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show P469 in e-court. Thank you. Can we please turn it around. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we can see that it says "Telegrams" in Latin alphabet, then it's followed by the number 28/34. It was probably marked by someone who classified it, it could be someone from the OTP, and your ERN number. And then we can see in Cyrillic "Atlantida" or "Atlantis." When we showed this to Danko Gojkovic he said he never wrote this, either the word "Telegrams" or the title "Atlantida," and that this was the first time that he ever saw that. On the basis of the witness told us and what I just told you, can you tell us how is it possible that this title may have come into being once it was already archived and was not anymore in the possession of Mr. Danko Gojkovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember Danko Gojkovic's testimony, he says that all the telegrams that had been sent by him or received by him were handed over to the command, the command of the Rogatica Brigade. I believe this binder was created in Rogatica Brigade command. I think, because, as we see, if you look at the following pages from the first page, there are some logistical documents and also the name of the assistant commander for the logistics of Rogatica Brigade. I think, I think, but I said I couldn't check it because the guy refused to be interviewed by me, that this binder could be created in the command of the Rogatica Brigade. And it's possible that this "Telegrami," "28/34" and "Atlantida" name were somewhere created on this level, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were all documents classified in this way in the Rogatica Brigade and also marked with secret names just like this one? As Danko worked in the command of the Rogatica Brigade, it would be normal for him to determine the titles for the documents which he wrote and classified and which you designated as Danko's documents, or was it someone else who wrote all this on the documents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also from the testimony of Danko Gojkovic and his interview, I remember that he didn't create any archive material, at least with this type of material, and everything that had been produced by him or sent by him or received by him had been sent to the command of Rogatica Brigade. What happened there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please answer the following question. Did Danko work at the command of the Rogatica Brigade and where was his office located, if you know? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Danko is -- this is communication officer of the Rogatica Brigade. His office was located, let's say, in the premises of the Rogatica Brigade command, but not in the building where the real command was located. This is the building next to the command, small building about 50, 100 metres from the command itself. I know this place. I've been there a few times, and this place has been described also by Danko Gojkovic and by other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, as an investigator, that if an organ or a department produces documents that they would have to keep them in their own records and not hand them over into the archives, because if anything is coded, there is the possibility that some of the secret information might leak out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is possible, but difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that a telegram or a code must not be used to transfer contents which are dictated aloud in a room where they're being typed out, precisely because of the possibility that the room is being wire-tapped and that in this way the key for a specific code might be found? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible in few cases, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you conclude on the basis of that that Danko was also not allowed to send anywhere the perforated tapes which he used or telegrams; and as for texts, that he had to return them to the organs which submitted them to him, that is to say, logistics department and so on and so forth? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is exactly what Danko did. You know, he handed over these documents to his commander -- to his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But Danko could not hand over the documents to his command when he was a member of the command. He would have to keep his own documents. He could hand something over to the Drina Corps. Is it perhaps that you are confusing his command with the Drina Corps command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not confusing Danko. Danko, this is ordinary soldier. He was the communication officer. He didn't take any particular role in the command. He was attached to the command as a communication officer who was ordinary soldier. It was not his role to keep any documents. He followed the rule established by the commander and his assistants in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaszczyk. This is your opinion. But I'm asking you if Danko says that he never saw a binder like this one with this title - and this is what he stated here in front of this Trial Chamber in this courtroom - could you tell us who could have produced this binder and when could it have been produced if it was not produced at the time when the documents were still in the possession of the cryptographer at the Rogatica Brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to Danko, who was the cryptographer in the Rogatica Brigade, he handed over all the documents or the dispatches which he received or has sent to the command and somebody in the command, I can only assume who it could be, created this binder. And also the first page, you're referring to this "Atlantida" page, whatever it's called, has been created over there in the command position, not by Danko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who it was who produced it? I also asked you whether all the documents from the logistics organ, reconnaissance organs, intelligence organs, and so on, had a code-name for the place of their documents, just as this one has the code-name "Atlantida"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I only can suspect, you know, who did -- who created this binder. You know, I thought that this was assistant commander for the logistics because in the following pages, the first pages of this "Atlantida" binder, we see documents with his handwriting, with his name on it, and I believe with his signature also. As I said, I tried to get information how this binder was created and he refused -- this man, he refused to talk to us. He showed up for our interview, but he refused to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will remind you that only the first three documents were produced by the logistics organs. The rest contains telegrams which were written by me and which you called "Atlantida." I wrote them while I was at the Rogatica Brigade. I wanted to know whether the logistics organ could keep the telegrams which were written by the security organ and which were recorded by the cryptographers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the position of the guy who is mentioned the first pages of this "Atlantida" binder was the assistant commander for the logistics of the Rogatica Brigade, but he could perform of the command officer also the duty as duty officer or office in charge in case if commander was not -- not of his area of responsibility. I don't know, he may have had access to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether he selected the documents in the same manner as ICTY, that is to say, you the investigators did, and then submitted it under these covers entitled "Atlantida," because this does not contain other documents except those that were tendered by the OTP, and does "Atlantida" contain any other documents? Can you please tell that to the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell that this binder was seized by us in this shape. I cannot say what the criterion the man used in creating this binder, I don't know it. I can confirm only that definitely this is the shape how this binder was seized or received by OTP. I seen this binder first time, I remember very clear, in Zagreb field office, when I arrived to Zagreb field office. When I opened the boxes I made the initial assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order to finish with this, who wrote it or did not, and who selected it or did not, can you please tell us the following. Was the title "Atlantida" and the words "Telegrams 28/34" written in the Prosecution's office? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. It was written at that time when we seized this material -- I mean before that time, of course. Whether it was in Rogatica command, whether it was in Drina Corps, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show document 125. Thank you. Could we please show the Exhibit P125. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Tolimir. Now please repeat because your microphone was switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document which we saw last time. I will ask the witness whether he can recognise this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us why you, or a representative of the OTP, it does not matter, decided that precisely this document would be discussed during your testimony even though the entire collection of the Drina Corps has more than 300.000 pages? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is self-explanatory. It's talking about -- saying about the important issues and this is why we selected this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please answer another question now. How come that this document is not in the "Atlantida" collection? How do you explain that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, this document is not in the "Atlantida" collection? It is in the "Atlantida" collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But when you testified previously you said that it was found in Zvornik. Is that correct or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, General, I am getting confused a little bit. Did I say that this document was seized in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It doesn't matter. It is irrelevant. I can rephrase the question so I wouldn't go on confusing you. Could this document have been placed in the Drina Corps archives in Zvornik or in any other place which you mentioned that the archives went through, from Vlasenica through Bijeljina, Sokolac, Mali Zvornik, and Gornji Milanovac, Banja Luka, and Zagreb. So could it happen that this document may have been added to the archives in any of these locations because it's not recorded in any of the log-books? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can exclude that this document was added to this collection in Zagreb, Banja Luka, since the entire collection was in the possession of the ICTY. I can exclude this possibility for sure, 100 per cent sure. But of course, everything is possible that it was added somewhere later, but I don't think so. I don't see any reason why it should be done in this way. But physically it is possible because we had no control of this documentation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me first of all whether this document has a log number; and if so, what is this number?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean original log number? I don't see an original log number here in this document. This is our ICTY number, it's ERN number over -- on it, and also signature and date of communication officer from Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During your testimony you interpreted some of the registration numbers of documents, and, inter alia, you said that the registration number itself could show whether a document was an urgent one and the like, whether it was an order or something else. Can you tell us, as this document does not contain any of these characteristics in the heading, it doesn't say either "military secret" or "strictly confidential" or anything, can you say whether it was registered in any log-book of the Drina Corps, a brigade or corps, or any kind of log-book whatsoever? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then conclude, on the basis of your answers and on the basis of the facts, that it was never registered anywhere as either a military secret or something strictly confidential even though you say that it was encoded? We cannot even see that it was encoded as there is no trace of the teletypist.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that we can conclude that, but this is possible also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it usual to note the date, the time, and the marking whether a document is internal or public or confidential or strictly confidential in the upper left-hand corner of the document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is usual. Yeah, you're right, this is usual. Usually the documents have the number, the date, information about sensitivity of this document, all this type of information, but this document has not. But in fact we don't know. Maybe -- maybe this information was handed over to communication officer orally or maybe it was another paper also, the cover paper of this document. I don't know how he received this paper. He couldn't explain it because he doesn't remember this particular document, I mean the communication officer Danko Gojkovic. He remembers only, you know, based of his signature and handwritings that he sent these documents on the 13th July 1995 and at 1510 minutes -- hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As Danko cannot remember the contents or anything and, as you say, he processed it, is it then logical that when something is brought in to be encrypted to a place where only secret military information is being typed, as this was wartime, and as this type of document was not transmitted by fax or any other means that the enemy could find out, would it be normal that such a document would be signed by the person who was sending it so that the receiver would know that it was sent by so and so and on behalf of whom it was being sent? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be signed or could not, but if the communication officer receiving these documents from the command or somebody who may pass this type of documents to the communication office, it is logical also for him that he's obligated to send this document as soon as possible. And of course, there is no information about number of the document, log number, or whether this is document strictly confidential or not. But it -- for sure this information should be on the typed version of this document which was sent by teleprinter. Unfortunately, we don't have teleprinter version of this document, but as we see, as we got it from Danko Gojkovic it had been sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you just said, Danko does not remember the contents of the document nor who gave it to him or when. He just remembers that his signature, which we can see at the left-hand bottom corner, is written on this page. But there is no signature of the sending party. On the basis of all this, when there is no registration number, it is not logged, it was not signed by the sending party, then does a cryptographer express his doubt that he might be sending a telegram that he should not send because it includes some activities that should be carried out and which could cause major consequences? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, first of all, what was your question? It was more a statement rather than a question. And the other thing is I was very cautious to interrupt you because you were dealing with this document, but we are running out of time. We must have our break now. We are ten minutes later than expected. We must have our first break now and resume ten minutes past 11.00, and then you could think about rephrasing your last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, I was asking you about the elements that demonstrate that the document is authentic. You just mentioned the signature in the lower left-hand corner, but I asked you whether there were any doubts with the sender as to whether he was sending something for which he had received no authorisation. Thank you. And I'll complete my question by saying: Would it be logical for Danko to ask himself who had signed this document since it hasn't been registered, it hadn't been stamped? There are no elements that show that this document is an authentic one.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This depends who handed this document to Danko to send it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we here, in the court, assume that someone gave it to him who had authority over Danko, so he had to send each and every telegram, regardless on whose behalf or in whose name that telegram was?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you then perhaps tell us who this person that you have in mind is?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be somebody -- officer in charge from the command of the Rogatica Brigade or who had authority over Danko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that an encryptor's superior is only the commander because an encryptor works in an autonomous manner. There are only one or two such individuals in a given command and they form an integral part of that command? Are you aware of that fact? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the commander, he is the main officer in charge of Danko, but it could be also another officer authorised by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to speculate. I just want to ask you the following. Documents that are encrypted are considered to be the most confidential ones; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As an investigator and a professional policeman, are you aware of the fact that each and every document that is being encrypted leaves certain traces, traces such as those left by the finger-prints of a person who has touched certain objects? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise to the interpreters. As an investigator and a professional policeman, are you aware of the fact that when investigating documents that are being encrypted and sent, there are three ways in which a person checking such documents can verify whether these documents are in fact authentic or not? Thank you. Since you're not answering the question, I'll rephrase it. Do you know that there are three elements that allow one to confirm the authenticity of the contents of some document that has been sent through a teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean three elements? Could you specify it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I can. Finger-prints for everyone are different, and as a policeman you must be aware of the fact. And similarly, each and every machine leaves behind its own individual traces. For example, if you have a look at the document that we see on the left, if it has to be transported to a tape with all the punctuation, with all its contents, then the trace of the typewriter will be recorded on the teleprinter and this will then have to be identical to the previous two documents that go through the teleprinter. Are you aware of that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The document that we can see here on the screen, it doesn't have a signature or a stamp and so on and so forth, should this document have also been accompanied by another two copies after it had gone through the teleprinter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document has been typed out on the teleprinter by teleprinter operator, and of course, the person who received this document printed out his own version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If this is one version, the document we see now - and you claim that it's the original - if the second version was typed out by the teleprinter operator, then the marks or traces left by that machine must be different from the marks left by this original document. And then each teleprinter has a certain perforated tape or band that contains a third set of traces left by the document. So in each case there are three ways in which the authenticity of a document can be checked. Are you aware of that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this document has been typed out on the tele -- of the typewriter machine, not on the teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where the teleprinter mark is left if it is sent by teleprinter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know where the markings of the teleprinter is located if it's sent by teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure whether I understood you correctly. I know how a teleprinter looked and more or less, you know, how it operate, but I never worked on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for saying you didn't understand me. Have a look at the document to the left. Danko receives it, the sender sends it to him and he receives it; is that correct? Thank you. When this document is typed out on a typewriter, does it arrive in this form? Does it arrive in Danko hands through the teleprinter in this form?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document -- Danko received this document in this form as we see here in -- looking at his signature and information when he sent these documents out, but of course he typed out this document on the teleprinter. It was definitely in different form, it should be different form of this document. But unfortunately, we don't have this version of this document typed out on teleprinter. We have only the version of the document typed on telewriter -- or the typewriter. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does a teleprinter leave a copy that is identical to this document that has to be sent to the receiver? So does the teleprinter produce such a copy?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from that identical copy, does the teleprinter also leave behind a second tape with the imprint of these letters in electronic form?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does each document that is being sent by the operator have to have those three copies after the processing phase has been completed by the operator? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. It should be three copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And the copy that the operator receives for processing, does that copy have to be sent back to be checked? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand, should be sent back to be checked -- checked by whom? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the operator who receives a copy from the sender, does he have to send back that paper to the sender? So as a rule, does he have to send it back to the person from whom he received the document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Danko Gojkovic through his testimony explained the procedure regarding the documents, you know, who was supposed to be sent by him by teleprinter. And he says that the documents, after sending out by him, were handed over back to the command, but I don't remember whether he mentioned any particular person or not. But he says that it was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me the following. Would Danko keep this document typed on the machine as evidence that he had sent the telegram or did he have evidence in the form of the copy that was created by the device? As a policeman, if you are looking into ways in which a teleprinter had been put to inappropriate use, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking about my reaction? What I would do with this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I don't have to ask you personally, but what would a policeman, any policeman, have to look for to determine that the contents of a telegram received by a processor, to determine that the telegram had been sent to the required address, to determine that someone hadn't forgotten -- to determine that someone hadn't forgotten to send that telegram. If you were, for example, investigating a criminal case, a crime that had been committed, what would you do in such cases?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are quite limited to investigate this particular issue because we have access to this document, this one document. We have no access to the teleprinter, we have no access to the tape from this particular teleprinter. We have no access to the full archive of the -- of, I believe, Drina Corps collection. We have no access to the log-book of documents which were sent by communication officer from Rogatica Brigade in this particular case. And I don't think that we may do much more, you know, than we did in this document, just to find out how this document was sent out. Except, of course, interviewing the person mentioned in the document, that is Danko Gojkovic, and trying to find out the person who could collect this documentation in one this particular binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you didn't want to answer the question - perhaps you don't know the answer - what constitutes better evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just going to try to put a stop to that. There's no need to characterise the witness's testimony and cast aspersions on the witness. He's answered fully a number of very similar questions about a topic which the Trial Chamber has already heard a volume of testimony from the teleprinter operator himself, Mr. Gojkovic, who Mr. Blaszczyk has told you a number of times he personally interviewed. So if there's going to be further questioning along this line, I think it's more respectful of the witness not to allege that he's failing or trying not to answer the question when he clearly has over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I realise as well you said: "Since you didn't want to answer the question ..." I think that was not an appropriate statement. This witness is here for a long time answering all the questions to him. I don't see any sign that he is not willing to answer the question. You should be careful by such a statement. Please carry on, but try to use your time sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Blaszczyk, you are an investigator, that's why I'm putting this question to you. Don't take it personally. You are an investigator. But would a copy from a teleprinter constitute better evidence or would a copy on a perforated track be better evidence if -- if the document had been typed on an ordinary machine? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it would be -- I don't know whether better, but it would be additional evidence, you know, confirming this particular dispatch. Whether this is better evidence or worse evidence is up to the Trial Chamber to decide. But I would like to have a copy of this teleprinter version of this document, also the tape, I would like definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber shall decide as to what constitutes better evidence, which copy constitutes better evidence. I won't ask you anything else about that. Let's see what a different witness says about this document. Danko said he couldn't remember. He said that he only knew that his signature was in a lower left-hand corner, so let's see what another witness has to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness the following document: 1D116. It's the transcript from the Popovic case. The transcript page is 15262, and in the e-court system the relevant number is 32. I'll read out the relevant part of the transcript. It's in English and my legal advisor has provided me with a Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can now see it in English on the screen. Let's just find the page. While waiting for that, I'll start reading out the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I was told that there is no page 32 in e-court. Please check that again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks. We'll check that immediately on the basis of the copy that has been made. Thank you. My legal advisor will check the page. This is the transcript from the testimony that Colonel Savcic gave. You don't have his signature on this document, but he's mentioned. When we see what he says and compare it to what Danko said, I'll put a few questions to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, we would like to have the correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- so that we can finish discussing this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We would like to have the correct part of the transcript on the screen. Can you indicate again which is the page number and the line number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript page is 15262, 15262, and in the e-court system it is page 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is no page 32. On the screen we have page 32776. Are you referring to that page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Is it sufficient to provide you with the transcript -- the page of the transcript, 15262?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, General Tolimir has quoted the correct transcript page. If it helps, it's the 12th of September, 2007, that's the date of the testimony of Mr. Savcic and his testimony on this topic continues from 15262 through 15265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, this is 65 ter 1D118, not 1D116.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Thank you, and I apologise for the delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll now read out only part of the transcript, lines 7 to 14, for example. The witness, Savcic, says the following: "... my name is here, but not my signature [as interpreted]. I've already told you that I can't remember having drafted this document, and there are several other reasons for which I still don't believe that I drafted it. Above all, the title says: 'IKM Forward Command Post of the 65th Protection Regiment,' et cetera, 'Borike, 1400 hours.' I did not set up that forward command post. I just led part of the unit that was there. There is no date," he probably means on the document. "This document doesn't have the format of a telegram ..." And then he continues to say in lines 16 and 17: "... I cannot suggest something to the commander of the Main Staff or to his deputy, because I'm not an assistant commander in a position to make suggestions to him. I'm just a subordinate who executes the orders he is given." Then lines 19 to 24, he says: "Furthermore, you see, after the first sentence, it says: "'Assistant commander of the Main Staff of the VRS for intelligence and security proposes the following measures.' "So the assistant commander proposes, and I'm the one who writes things down. If he is the one who makes proposals, why isn't he the one who writes them?" And then General Savcic says on page 15263 of the transcript, lines 1 to 5: "That's something that I know. So I cannot say with any certainty that I drafted this, as dictated by Tolimir, but I also cannot exclude this possibility with 100 per cent certainty. All I can say is that this document was never received by the military police commander. The military police commander never acted on it." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is as follows --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I should put the question now or whether Mr. Thayer would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait a moment. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if General Tolimir wants to ask a question at this point, I think in all fairness to the witness and frankly to the record that he continue reading the transcript and give the witness an opportunity to read the transcript through page 15264. It will save time. I don't have to put it back up on re-direct and waste more court time to place this in context. So I just ask that the witness be given an opportunity to read 15263, and the Trial Chamber as well, and 15264.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Tolimir, do you agree with the proposal of Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not familiar with the contents. I said that my legal advisor only translated this part of the transcript. Since from the beginning of the trial I never received the transcript of any conferences or trials. I received nothing, but I should. So I don't know English so I could only read out what was translated for me. I have nothing against Mr. Thayer reading this out because I'm in favour of all the arguments being presented that can help us to determine the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against any sort of contents that would bring us to the truth. So I would kindly ask Mr. Thayer to read it out and the interpreters to interpret it for me because I do not have a translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness could read the relevant part of the transcript. I think it was page 15264. Mr. Thayer, can you indicate again which portion you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You had it correct, Mr. President, 15264.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's really the whole page that places in context the statement that General Tolimir read about Major Malinic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise, but I haven't read out anything about Major Malinic. I read out what Savcic stated at the court for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think now we are a little confused, and perhaps we leave it for the cross-examination. It's perhaps more appropriate and practical so that Mr. Tolimir should now put a question to the witness to that portion he was quoting. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question for the witness is this: As for the arguments noted by Milomir Savcic in the part of the transcript which I read out to you, are they convincing enough to show that the document which you showed here is inauthentic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, but who is convincing enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
